slides.title: Turning browser features off
slides.summary: Permissions-Policy declares which powerful features your page and each iframe may use.
body: Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy) is a response header that enables or disables browser features such as the camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and fullscreen, for your page and for each iframe.

ul: Least privilege: if your app never uses the camera, turn it off. An XSS payload or third-party script then can't ask for it.
Control embeds: a feature disabled for your page is disabled for every iframe inside it too.
Per-frame grants: the iframe allow attribute delegates a feature to one specific frame.

body: <mark>Disable every powerful feature you don't use, and delegate the rest only to the frames that need them.</mark>

body.text: Feature-Policy was the original name, with a different syntax (camera 'none'). It was renamed Permissions-Policy with structured-header syntax (camera=()). Use the new header; the old one is legacy.

Chromium browsers support the header for many features. Firefox and Safari support the iframe allow attribute but only part of the header, so check each feature on MDN and don't rely on the header alone.

figure.alt: A page at shop.example sends Permissions-Policy: camera=(), geolocation=(self), payment=(self "https://pay.example"). Inside the page, the shop's own code can use geolocation and payment, but not the camera. An iframe from pay.example with allow="payment" can use payment, because the header lists that origin and the attribute delegates it; it cannot use geolocation. An iframe from ads.example gets nothing: no camera, no geolocation, no payment, even if it asks.

slides.title: Allowlist syntax
slides.summary: Each feature takes an allowlist: *, (), self, specific origins, and for iframes, src.
body: The header form is Permissions-Policy: feature=(allowlist), feature=(allowlist). The allowlist can be:

ul: *: allowed for this page and every iframe, whatever its origin. Rarely a good idea.
(): blocked everywhere, including your own page. The iframe allow equivalent is 'none'.
self: your own origin and same-origin iframes only.
"https://maps.example": a specific origin. Quoted in the header, unquoted in the allow attribute.
src (iframe allow only, and the default there): allowed if the frame's document comes from the origin in its src.

body: * and () must be used alone; self and src can be combined with origins.
<mark>An iframe gets a feature only if both the page's header and the iframe's allow attribute permit it.</mark>

body.note: Example: a clinic site embeds a video-consultation widget. Only that frame needs the camera and microphone; the map frame needs geolocation; nothing else needs either.

cells.text: Header and attribute both allow it
Different origin; self doesn't cover it

slides.title: Testing a policy
slides.summary: Watch the console for violations, inspect the active policy in DevTools, and test in more than one browser.
body: Imagine an embedded promo widget that quietly calls navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(). With geolocation=() in your header, the call fails as if the user had denied permission, and no prompt appears.

ul: Console: Chromium logs a “Permissions policy violation” message naming the feature and the frame.
DevTools → Application → Frames → top: the Permissions Policy section lists allowed and disabled features for that frame. Select an iframe to see its own effective policy.
Network panel: check the response headers of the document to confirm the header actually shipped.
Cross-browser: Chromium enforces the header for many features; Firefox and Safari mainly honour the iframe allow attribute, so use both.

body: <mark>Write code that handles a denied feature gracefully: a blocked API behaves like a user saying no.</mark>
